title: Controlled Microfluidic Environment for Dynamic Investigation of Red Blood Cell Aggregation
protocol: Design the microchannel geometry using a Computer Aided Design (CAD) software.
Print the configuration on a transparency photo-mask.
Spin coat an epoxy based negative photo-resist on a silicon wafer at 2,000 rpm for 30 sec to obtain the desired microchannel depth (60 µm).
Expose the wafer and the photo-mask under a UV lamp at 650 mJ/cm² for 70 sec.
Immerse the silicon piece into a developer to remove excess of photo-resist.
Mix a silicon based elastomer and a curing agent at a ratio of 10:1 to create a solution of poly-dimethyl-siloxane (PDMS).
Put the PDMS solution in a vacuum chamber to degas.
Pour it into the mold and heat it at 60 °C for 90 min to create microchannels.
Bond the individual channels to a glass slide using oxygen plasma bonding for 90 sec.
Collect blood from healthy volunteer donors after ethics committee approval.
Treat the collected blood with EDTA in collection tubes (7.2 mg EDTA per 4 ml of blood).
Centrifuge the blood samples for 10 min at 1,400 x g to separate blood constituents.
Observe three layers: RBC layer at the bottom, buffy coat on top of RBC layer, and plasma layer on top.
Collect blood plasma using a blood pipette after first centrifugation.
Avoid contact with the buffy coat during plasma collection.
Dispose of the buffy coat in a container with 10% diluted bleach.
Add 3 ml of PBS pH 7.4 to each tube with the remaining RBC layer.
Ensure proper balance of the centrifuge.
Centrifuge tubes at 1,400 x g (3,000 rpm) for 10 min.
Dispose of the PBS after the second centrifugation.
Remove any remaining buffy coat present.
Repeat steps to yield clean RBCs.
Mix required amount of clean RBCs with plasma to obtain RBC-suspensions with corresponding hematocrit levels (5%, 10%, and 15%).
Check hematocrits using a microcentrifuge.
Introduce RBC-suspensions into the double Y-microchannel.
Add 60 µl of fluorescent tracer particles solution into each 1 ml RBC-suspension tube.
Prepare PBS pH 7.4 solution.
Add 60 µl of fluorescent tracer particles solution to 1 ml of PBS solution.
Use two glass syringes of 25 µl and 100 µl to insert fluids into the microchannel.
Connect the microchannel to the syringes via tubing and connectors fitting the entry holes.
Fill the glass syringes using the pressure difference between the fluid container and the syringe.
Ensure no bubbles are present in the system.
Place the microchannel on an inverted microscope stage connected to a high speed camera and a µPIV system.
Program the syringe pump to desired flow rates (e.g., Q = 2 µl/hr for blood, Q = 8 µl/hr for PBS).
Insert both fluids into the double Y-microchannel each from a different entry branch at different flowrates.
Change the pump flowrate to test different shear rates while maintaining the appropriate ratio between the two branches.
Wait for the flow to reach steady state before acquiring measurements.
Visually inspect high speed camera images for smooth flow.
Visualize RBCs using the high speed camera.
Connect the camera to a computer for control and recording of images.
Acquire several images once fluid flows reach steady state.
Determine an optimal camera exposure time for clear image quality.
Enhance image contrast using histogram equalizer method.
Convert grayscale images into binary images.
Set a threshold value ranging from 0 to 1 for pixel conversion.
Fill the holes corresponding to gaps within one aggregate for better results.
Detect cells by determining neighboring white pixels in the binary image so that adjacent cells are associated as aggregates.
Label different aggregates detected and convert the binary image into a red-green-blue (RGB) image for better visualization.
Combine original frames with each of the corresponding processed images to verify the efficiency of the image processing technique.
Calculate the area of each aggregate detected in the frame based on the number of pixels detected.
Determine a conversion factor using a calibration reticule, then convert results to µm² based on lens magnification used.
Average the aggregate sizes detected in each frame and average the results for all frames to obtain the average aggregate size for each recording of RBC-suspensions.
Calculate the area of one RBC to determine an estimated number of RBCs within each detected aggregate.
Using these results, calculate the distribution of the percentage of RBCs within each aggregate as a function of the aggregate sizes.
Take all necessary precautions before turning on the laser.
Turn on the system, camera, and laser.
Calibrate the camera based on lens magnification using a microscale of 10 μm precision.
Start the laser and visualize particles in both fluids.
Find the middle plane of the microchannel by focusing on the fastest particles.
Set the dt (time interval between two consecutive frames) to ensure proper particle displacement.
Start recording the flow with the software set to acquire 100 pairs of images, 5 msec apart.
Process recordings acquired using the cross-correlation method with imaging software.
Determine if images require pre-processing for better data processing.
Choose correlation window size and shape.
Select percentage of image overlapping.
Discretize pair of images into small windows called correlation windows.
Follow displacement of particles in each window.
Express results as an average velocity field from 100 image pairs.
Calculate Root Mean Square (RMS) error in velocity.
Extract a velocity profile at the channel outlet from processed data.
Average the velocity field in space for better profile.
Turn off the laser once all measurements and processing are performed.
Shut down the software system.
Shut down the cameras.
Shut down the moving stage.
Shut down the computers.
Shut down the laser.
Detect blood thickness in the microchannel based on high-speed camera recordings.
Average all frames to obtain a background image of the video recording.
Delimit the blood layer for each hematocrit condition (5%, 10%, and 15%).
Obtain velocity values corresponding to the blood layer thickness.
Calculate shear rate by dividing velocity value by blood layer thickness.
